label: Clear_Cell_RCC
answer_markdown:
## Key Facts
- Clear cell renal cell carcinoma (CCRCC) accounts for about 80% of renal cell carcinoma cases.
- Typically presents with a golden-yellow cut surface due to abundant clear cytoplasm with lipids.
- Common genetic alteration: loss of chromosome 3p and mutations in the VHL gene.
- Often detected incidentally on imaging.
- Associated with von Hippel-Lindau syndrome in familial cases.
- Occurs across a wide age range, 8–88 years, and is linked to end-stage renal disease (ESRD) [WHO](https://storage.googleapis.com/pathology-hub-0/WHO/WHO_HTML/GU/Clear_Cell_Papillary_Renal_Cell_Tumour.html) and [Pathoutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/kidneytumormalignantacquiredcysticRCC.html).

## Terminology
- Clear cell renal cell carcinoma (CCRCC).
- Synonyms include "conventional renal cell carcinoma."
- Not to be confused with "clear cell papillary renal cell tumor" or "clear cell adenocarcinoma."

## Essential and Desirable Diagnostic Criteria
- **Essential:**
  - Clear cell morphology with abundant clear cytoplasm.
  - Architectural patterns: nests, sheets, and tubules.
  - High-grade nuclear features often present.
- **Desirable:**
  - Presence of necrosis and hemorrhage.
  - Vascular invasion and extension beyond the renal capsule.

## Etiology/Pathogenesis
- Genetic basis: loss of 3p and VHL gene mutations.
- Other factors include increased reactive oxygen species and depressed immune function in renal failure [Pathoutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/kidneytumormalignantacquiredcysticRCC.html).

## Clinical Issues
- **Epidemiology:**
  - Represents 80% of all renal cell carcinomas.
  - Peaks in the sixth to seventh decade of life.
  - Male predominance.
- **Site:**
  - Originates in the renal cortex.
- **Natural History:**
  - Indolent to aggressive behavior based on stages.
- **Prognosis:**
  - Depends on stage and grade; localized tumors have a better outcome.
- Tumors are multifocal in 20% of cases and bilateral in 25% [WHO](https://storage.googleapis.com/pathology-hub-0/WHO/WHO_HTML/GU/Clear_Cell_Papillary_Renal_Cell_Tumour.html).

## Macroscopic
- Golden-yellow cut surface due to lipid content.
- Often encapsulated, multiple cysts may be present.
- Variegated appearance with areas of necrosis and hemorrhage.

## Microscopic
- Primarily clear cells with rounded nuclei and prominent nucleoli.
- Tubular or alveolar patterns.
- Delicate vascular network, often described as "chicken-wire" vasculature.
- Necrosis and hemorrhage may be present, increasing the grade.

## Ancillary Tests
- **IHC Panel:**
  - Positive: PAX8, RCC, CD10, CAIX.
  - Variable: CK7.
- **Molecular/genetics:**
  - VHL gene mutations and 3p loss are common alterations.

## Differential Diagnosis

| Feature/Marker | Clear Cell RCC | Papillary RCC | Chromophobe RCC | Clear Cell Papillary RCC | Rhabdoid Tumour of the Kidney |
|----------------|----------------|---------------|-----------------|--------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Architecture   | Alveolar/nests | Papillary     | Solid           | Papillary/tubular        | Rhabdoid or solid             |
| Cytology       | Clear cells    | Foam cells    | Pale cells      | Clear cells              | Eosinophilic cytoplasm        |
| VHL Mutation   | Yes            | No            | No              | No                       | No                            |
| IHC - CK7      | Variable       | Positive      | Positive        | Strongly positive        | Variable                      |
| IHC - CD10     | Positive       | Variable      | Negative        | Positive                 | Positive                      |

- Rhabdoid tumour of the kidney may also demonstrate overlapping features with RCC subtypes [WHO](https://storage.googleapis.com/pathology-hub-0/WHO/WHO_HTML/GU/Rhabdoid_Tumour_Of_The_Kidney.html).

cards.excerpt: Entity: Collecting duct carcinoma Section: microscopic CDC typically shows tubular and tubulopapillary architectural patterns with irregular, infiltrating glands and associated desmoplastic stroma. Solid nested or sheet-like, trabecular, cord-like individual cells, as well as microcystic patterns, may also be present; a subset show an infiltrative nodular papillary component. The tumour edge is poorly defined, with tumour cells infiltrating between tubules and glomeruli of the adjacent renal parenchyma, which may show dysplasia or atypia within uninvolved tubules. There is often a prominent inflammatory reaction including a neutrophil infiltrate within and around the tumour. Lymphovascular invasion and regional lymph node involvement are common at nephrectomy. The cells exhibit high-grade nuclear features, usually with eosinophilic cytoplasm, but they can be clear or amphophilic. Cells lining tubules are often cuboidal, although columnar and hobnail cells are common. Nuclei are large, vesicular, and highly pleomorphic, with prominent nucleoli. cards.entity_name: Clear cell sarcoma of the kidney
cards.excerpt: Entity: Clear cell sarcoma of the kidney definition: Clear cell sarcoma of the kidney (CCSK) is a rare malignant renal tumour of childhood characterized histologically by variably clear tumour cells and distinctive arborizing fibrovascular septa, and molecularly by BCOR mutations or YWHAE::NUTM2 gene fusion. related_terminology: Not recommended: bone-metastasizing renal tumour of childhood. essential_and_desirable_diagnostic_criteria: Essential: characteristic histomorphology of ovoid tumour cells with nuclear and/or cytoplasmic clearing at least focally, distinctive arborizing fibrovascular septa, and immunoreactivity for cyclin D1 and BCOR. Desirable: features for cases with atypical histomorphology or immunophenotype include molecular identification of BCOR exon 15 ITD or of YWHAE::NUTM2 or BCOR::CCNB3 gene fusion.

cards.title: Clear cell papillary renal cell tumour
cards.entity_name: Clear cell papillary renal cell tumour
cards.excerpt: Entity: Clear cell papillary renal cell tumour Section: clinical The vast majority of these tumours are incidentally detected. --- The tumour accounts for approximately 3% of cases of renal cell carcinoma (RCC) in adults, with an age range of 8–88 years. The tumours can occur in end-stage renal disease. Tumours of identical morphology that occur in patients with von Hippel–Lindau syndrome appear genomically related to clear cell RCC and distinct from CCPRCT. In 20% and 25% of cases, patients have multifocal and bilateral renal tumours, respectively, and in > 50% of these patients, there is a discordant subtype.

cards.title: Rhabdoid tumour of the kidney
cards.excerpt: Entity: Rhabdoid tumour of the kidney Section: ancillary_studies For rhabdoid tumour of the kidney with SMARCA4 inactivation, SMARCA4 (BRG1) immunohistochemistry may be used; this shows a loss of nuclear staining in tumour cells and normal expression in all other cells. Other than by loss of SMARCB1 (INI1) immunostaining, rhabdoid tumour of the kidney and indeed all rhabdoid tumours have a diverse pattern of immunoreactivity, including multiple keratins and vimentin, but also SMA, synaptophysin, and GFAP. Nonspecific polyphenotypic patterns for other antibodies may occur due to trapping of antibodies in hyaline inclusions such as EMA and pancytokeratin. Importantly, over half of rhabdoid tumours show CD99 expression, which may add to the morphological confusion with Ewing sarcoma. Although differential diagnoses are limited in cases with typical morphology and immunohistochemistry, cellular mesoblastic nephroma, plump cell pattern, and clear cell sarcoma of the kidney may be considered. Several renal cell carcinoma morphologies, including clear cell renal cell carcinoma and renal medullary carcinoma, may show rhabdoid morphology with or without SMARCB1 (INI) loss.

cards.title: Acquired cystic disease associated — Epidemiology
cards.excerpt:
ACD typically occurs after dialysis for end stage renal disease (ESRD)
Incidence of ACD progressively increases with duration of dialysis: from 10 - 20% after 3 years to > 90% after 10 years of hemodialysis or peritoneal dialysis
Overall incidence of ACD-RCC is 3 - 7% in end stage kidney, which is 100 times greater than in the general population (Kidney Int 2002;61:2201)
ACD-RCC is the most common RCC subtype in both ACD (40%) and ESRD (30%)
Other tumors that occur in end stage kidneys include clear cell papillary renal cell tumors and clear cell, papillary and chromophobe RCCs

cards.entity_name: Clear cell papillary renal cell tumour
cards.excerpt: Entity: Clear cell papillary renal cell tumour Section: diagnostic_molecular_pathology There are specific molecular pathological features diagnostic of this tumour. Importantly, this tumour lacks chromosome 3p loss and alterations of VHL characteristic of clear cell RCC, and no mutations in TSC1, TSC2, MTOR, or ELOC (TCBE1) (all characteristic of RCC with fibromyomatous or leiomyomatous stroma) have been reported.

cards.title: Mixed epithelial and stromal tumour of the kidney
cards.entity_name: Mixed epithelial and stromal tumour of the kidney
cards.excerpt: Entity: Mixed epithelial and stromal tumour of the kidney Section: ancillary_studies The stromal component is typically positive for actin, desmin, CD10, ER, and PR and frequently the luteinized stromal cells express inhibin and calretinin. Cathepsin K is negative. The epithelial component is PAX2/8-positive. Immunohistochemistry is helpful in the exclusion of renal synovial sarcoma, clear cell papillary tumour, and tubulocystic renal cell carcinoma.

cards.excerpt: Entity: PEComa Section: differential_diagnosis In childhood, the diagnosis of PEComa may be extremely challenging because of a relatively large differential diagnosis, which differs depending on the tumour site and can include clear cell sarcoma of soft tissue (also known as melanoma of soft parts), alveolar soft part sarcoma, smooth muscle tumours, MiT-family translocation renal cell carcinoma, clear cell sarcoma of the kidney, gastrointestinal stromal tumour, and metastatic melanoma.

cards.title: Acquired cystic disease associated — Solid and cystic hemorrhagic neoplasmMicroscopic (histologic) description
cards.excerpt:
Highly variable architecture: cribriform, microcystic, sieve-like, tubulopapillary and solid patterns
Cells with large nuclei, prominent nucleoli and abundant granular eosinophilic cytoplasm with intracytoplasmic holes and intercytoplasmic lumina due to crystal depositions
Intratumoral calcium oxalate crystals are very common but not necessary for diagnosis (Am J Surg Pathol 2005;29:443)
May be nodules arising from cyst walls or solid masses separate from cysts (Am J Surg Pathol 2013;37:1469)

cards.title: Acquired cystic disease associated — Molecular / cytogenetics description
cards.excerpt:
Comparative genomic microarray and FISH studies reveal gains and losses of multiple chromosomes (Am J Surg Pathol 2013;37:1469)
Gains of sex chromosomes and gains of 3, 7, 16, 17 (Eur Urol 2016;70:93)
High prevalence of gains of Y, 3 and 16 distinguishes from papillary RCC, which also has gains in chromosomes 7 and 17 (Eur Urol 2016;70:93)
Recurrent KMT2C or TSC2 gene mutations (Am J Surg Pathol 2020;44:1479)

cards.title: Renal cell carcinoma (RCC) — Lymph node, retroperitoneal, biopsy
cards.excerpt:
Metastatic carcinoma, suggestive of renal origin (see comment)
Comment: Sections of the retroperitoneal biopsy show the presence of metastatic tumor cells with abundant clear cytoplasm. A panel of immunohistochemistry stains show tumor cells to be positive for CD10 and RCC Ma, while being negative for CK7, CK20, PAX8, CD117 and CAIX. While the immunohistochemistry profile is not entirely concordant with a renal primary, especially with negative PAX8 and CAIX, the positivity of both CD10 and RCC Ma would suggest possibility of renal primary in the context of known history of renal cell carcinoma. Clinical and radiological correlation is recommended.

cards.title: Clear cell papillary renal cell tumor — Etiology
cards.excerpt:
Etiology is unclear; lacks genetic modifications and driver mutations frequently associated with other renal cell carcinomas (RCC)
First described in association with ESRD, particularly acquired cystic disease of the kidney (ACDK) (Am J Surg Pathol 2006;30:141)
It is now known that most cases arise sporadically, with no evidence of somatic VHL gene inactivation or chromosome 3p loss, unlike clear cell renal cell carcinoma (CCRCC) (Arch Pathol Lab Med 2019;143:1154)
Believed to be associated with upregulation of the hypoxia inducible factor 1 pathway, similar to other RCCs but through a non-VHL dependent mechanism
Evidence suggests a shift away from respiratory metabolism, toward sorbitol pathway of tumorigenesis (Elife 2019;8:e38986)

cards.title: Unclassified — Clinical features
cards.excerpt:
Clinical presentation similar to other RCC subtypes (IARC: WHO Classification of Tumours of the Urinary System and Male Genital Organs, 4th Edition, 2016)

cards.title: Unclassified — Prognostic factors
cards.excerpt:
Outcome is often associated with grade, stage and clinicopathologic features known to be relevant in other forms of RCC (BJU Int 2012;110:786)
The majority of studies show that unclassified RCC is more aggressive with 1.6 - 1.7X the mortality of clear cell RCC (J Urol 2002;168:950, BJU Int 2007;100:802, BJU Int 2012;110:786), however one study showed that overall cancer specific survival is similar in matched cohorts after adjusting for grade, stage and other parameters (Urology 2010;76:580)
Despite that discrepancy, > 50% of high grade unclassified RCC are dead of disease within 2 years

cards.title: Unclassified — Molecular / cytogenetics description
cards.excerpt:
A study of 62 high grade unclassified RCCs revealed mutations in NF2 (18%), SETD2 (18%), BAP1 (13%), KMT2C (10%) and MTOR (8%) (Nat Commun 2016;7:13131)
Chromosome genomic array testing (array CGH) and single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) arrays are both useful tools in resolving 80 - 94% of unclassified RCCs with ~50% cases reclassified as clear cell RCC
Reclassified tumors show characteristic cytogenetic changes of certain subtype plus numerous additional copy number aberrations (Am J Surg Pathol 2009;33:1276)

cards.title: Papillary — Treatment
cards.excerpt:
Resection or ablation for localized disease
Selective MET kinase inhibitor, MET / VEGF inhibitor, multitargeted tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) and PD-1 / PDL1 inhibitors for advanced or metastatic disease (Curr Opin Urol 2022;32:344)
For advanced metastatic PRCC cabozantinib shows higher efficacy over sunitinib and other MET kinase inhibitors (Lancet 2021;397:695)

cards.title: ALK translocation — Affects children with sickle cell trait or adults without sickle cell trait
cards.excerpt:
In children, resembles renal medullary carcinoma: medulla centric with diffuse infiltrating growth, lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate, large polygonal discohesive or spindled cells, cytoplasmic vacuoles and vesicular nuclei
In adults, heterogeneous solid architecture, mucinous cribriform, signet ring and solid rhabdoid patterns, high grade eosinophilic cells with intracytoplasmic lumina
